Label: A to B
Description: The main road to Chainpur led from the bazaar around the bus stand through fields and into Chainpur’s main bazaar.

Label: See a visual expression of Islamic practice
Description: Beneath a depiction of the Kaba in Makkah and the dome of the Prophet’s Mosque in Madinah two of the most popular pilgrimage sites for Muslims worldwide were the Urdu words (from right to left) for fasting (roza), prayer (namaz), the profession of faith (tauhid), alms (zakat), and pilgrimage (hajj) to Makkah.  Notably, the words have emerged from the flames of dips, oil-fed lamps devotionally used by both Muslims and Hindus in South Asia.
Source Object: A to B cemetery detail detail detail mazars parallel 2000s.jpg

Label: See the established mazars (“tombs”) of two Sufis
Description: Two white-washed barrows have marked the burial place of the two Sufis while the wall helped both maintain the cleanliness of the site and make it more visible.
Parent: View a set of Sufi Muslim tombs
Source Object: A to B cemetery detail detail mazars 2000s.jpg

Label: View a set of Sufi Muslim tombs
Description: Enclosed by the white-washed protective walls were the tombs of two Sufis (revered Islamic figures).
Source Object: A to B cemetery detail extra 2 2000s.jpg

Label: See agricultural fields
Description: Villages are defined as much by the fields that surround them as by their habitations and other buildings.  Unsurprisingly, almost any land without a building on it is tilled, seeded, and harvested, as could be seen at right along the roadside.

Label: See a mark of devotion
Description: Devotees sometimes have marked their devotion to a dead Sufi by adorning a mazar with a chadar (“sheet”) covered in Islamic texts and/or images.
Source Object: A to B mazar same as 0458 CLOSE 2000s.jpg

Label: See the construction of Sufi mazars (“tombs”)
Description: This platform with its two barrows indicating the tombs of two Sufis has been under construction.  A Hindu devotee has cared for the tombs, maintaining their tidiness.  Practices involving Sufis, living and dead, have frequently involved a mélange of devotees drawn from different religious communities.
Source Object: A to B mazar under reconstruction by Hindu 2000s.jpg

Label: See the mandir and an open well
Description: The temple precinct’s open ground occasionally has served as a useful site to gather and work harvested crops.  However, workers carefully have kept respectfully clean the raised concrete plinth in the left background with its Shiv linga and accompanying image of Shiv’s devotee, Nandi the bull.  In the foreground was an open well of a sort necessary before tube wells gave easier access to aquifer water sources.
Source Object: A to B Shankar Mahadev Mandir detail oblong 2000s.jpg

Label: See Sri Gauri Shankar Mahadev Mandir (“temple”)
Description: A person wearing a cricket outfit has passed the entrance to a temple dedicated to the goddess Gauri and the gods Shiv and Vishnu.  The road pavement has disintegrated unevenly along its edges.  Devotees would make much effort to improve the temple in the coming decades.
Source Object: A to B with Shiv mandir BEST 2000s.jpg

Label: See a roadside tool maker and seller
Description: This storeowner and craftsman offered a variety of tools for home and agricultural use.  He fashioned wood implements and wood handles for metal tools.
Source Object: A to B wood tool maker 2000s.jpg

Label: Buy some tools
Description: Wooden rolling pins, hand blenders, and chapati rolling platforms can be purchased from this artisan along with metal ladles, bowls, and hoes.
Source Object: A to B wood tool maker CLOSE 2000s.jpg

Label: Find medication for leprosy and tuberculosis
Description: The wall-painted sign advertised for the local public hospital: “Everyone can get for free T.B. and leprosy medication at the government hospital.  Varanasi Service Center, Adhaura” [the latter refers to the bloc where the hospital stood].
Source Object: A to Bhabhua TB and leprosy sign 2000s.jpg

Label: Road to Bhabua
Description: The road from Chand village continues on to the town of Bhabhua, which Bhabhua (or Kaimur) district headquarters. The road is an important area traffic artery.  The crossroads with the main road from Chainpur serves as an essential bus stand.

Label: Thana to Chand village road
Description: The road from the town of Bhabhua to the village of Chand has been an important area traffic artery.  The crossroads with the main road from Chainpur has served as an essential bus stand.  However, at the turn of the century, the road was narrow at best and often suffered from vast potholes and crumbling pavement.  Shepherds lead their flock, sharing the well-worn road with towering Tata trucks.

Label: AA to BB
Description: A few businesses, like the tailor at left, have positioned themselves along the first few meters of this street leading from Chowk Bazaar before it gave way to residences.  The herringbone-patterned brick paving ensured that the street remained passable even during torrential monsoon rains.

Label: Visit a butcher’s shop (note: graphic image)
Description: M. Bahadur Khan offered a butchered goat to customers while the neighboring shop sold eggs.  Chainpur consumers of meat often see their meals at every stage of preparation, from slaughter onward.  Meanwhile, the small kiosk perched on legs of bricks represented a common type of shop for those without a building.

Label: Buy fish
Description: Surendra Ram offered fish in this impromptu spot after helping to bring in the catch from one of the several large water reservoirs found around the Chainpur nexus that serve as fish hatcheries.

Label: AA to D
Description: The north-south road from the bus stand terminates in Chowk Bazaar.  Chowk refers to a habitation’s major intersection.  In Chainpur, the road from the north intersects not only with the most important road leading east and west but also the entrance to the qila (“fort”) where the busiest Hindu temple stands beyond the large arch.

Label: See respect for an elder
Description: Above the shelves packed with merchandise, Arvind had hung a framed photograph of his father who previously ran the store.  It has been garlanded with a mala (a string of flowers) in a common gesture of reverence.
Parent: Visit a cloth store and social place
Source Object: AA to D Shyam Babu's father’s image 2000s.jpg

Label: See a Hanuman poster
Description: In the renowned epic Ramayan, the great god-hero Ram and his brother Lakshman fall dead to the overwhelming onslaught of their enemy Ravan, a powerful rakshas (demon).  Hanuman, Ram's devoted monkey follower, hears that a cure can be found on a Himalayan peak.  Through his tremendous strength, Hanuman carries the entire mountain vegetation and all to revive the brothers.  Many Hindus revere Hanuman as a paragon of devotion and heroism.
Parent: Visit a cloth store and social place
Source Object: AA to D Shyam Babu's Hanuman poster 2000s.jpg

Label: See the shop’s puja place
Description: Hindu merchants commonly place in their shops a pair of Lakshmi (left) and Ganesh (right) murtis (statues), dedicating a new set of murtis each Diwali holiday after cleaning out their shop thoroughly and often applying a fresh coat of whitewash inside and out.  Lakshmi is the Goddess of Wealth and Ganesh the Remover of Obstacles.  Behind the shrine appeared to be a picture of the deity couple Kirshna and Radha.
Parent: Visit a cloth store and social place
Source Object: AA to D Shyam Babu's puja sthan 2000s.jpg

Label: See the store’s role as a social place
Description: Friends of the storeowner, Arvind Chaurasiya, routinely stopped by to relax on the mattress-covered floor, reading newspapers and discussing current events even as customers came in and out transacting business without religious or jati (caste) distinction.  Cloth merchants commonly travelled along the Ganga River Valley endeavoring to maintain their stock’s diversity.
Parent: Visit a cloth store and social place
Source Object: AA to D Shyam Babu's store Chainpur Debate Society 2000s.jpg

Label: See a Durga poster
Description: Hundreds of millions of Hindus worship Durga (seen at center) or one of the many other manifestations of this devi (goddess).  Many devotees understand her as a fearsome antagonist of chaos and, at the same time, a loving mother figure.  In one narrative, the gods arm her with their separate, distinctive weapons because none of them could overwhelm a buffalo demon causing havoc. She ultimately subdues him, but not before transforming into the even fiercer Kali.
Parent: Visit a cloth store and social place
Source Object: AA to D Shyam Babu's store Devi poster 2000s.jpg

Label: Visit a cloth store and social place
Description: The Chaurasiya family has run this cloth and readymade clothing store for two generations.  It has served not only as a thriving business but as a social place for sharing news, views, and chai, especially among the storeowner’s friends.  A tailor offered services for those buying cloth, working his pedal-powered sewing machine.
Source Object: AA to D Shyam Babu's store enter 2000s.jpg

Label: AA to GG
Description: Trees rarely find purchase in the crowded area around Chowk Bazaar where vegetables, snacks, and bags of rice were all sold, while others offer different services, such as bicycle repair.  Bicycles were ubiquitous, a far less expensive and very versatile mode of transportation for a rural area.

Label: See the main bazaar from above
Description: A rooftop view shows the variety of construction styles with flat-roofed brick and concrete buildings, sloped terracotta-roofed, and dried mud plastered one-story buildings.  Stone pavers maintain a stable if clattering road throughout the bazaar.
Source Object: AA to GG main bazaar from above 1995.jpg

Label: B to A
Description: See a tonga and tractor A donkey-drawn tonga followed a farm tractor and trailer as they passed thatched-awnings along the road leading from Chowk in Chainpur to the bus stand.  This was the northern edge of the most densely settlement of the village’s habitations and businesses.

Label: See Islamic decorations
Description: A clockface chalked on this store’s door helped advertise the Golden Watch business.  The Islamic symbol of a crescent moon with star hung above a similarly chalked image of the Taj Mahal in Agra.  The artist included a view of the garden in which this most iconic of Indian buildings stands.  Meanwhile, the Arabic numbers above the door (“786”) have long represented the Islamic system of abjad that assigns letters in words to numbers as a form of religious arithmetic.  “786” has been particularly auspicious.
Source Object: B to FF (r) Taj on door 2000s.jpg

Label: B to FF
Description: A cycle rickshaw driver laboriously pedalled his customers on the road leading from Chowk in Chainpur to the bus stand.  This was the northern edge of the habitations and businesses in the most densely settlement of the village.

Label: Consider family planning
Description: This ruined wall painting counseled Indians to decrease population growth and used the nation-wide family planning icon of a family of four woman, man, boy, girl as a model of the “small family is a happy family” motto.  In 1952, India was among the first nations to initiate a voluntary family planning program for its whole population, although forced and pressured sterilizations of millions have occurred in two different periods since then.
Source Object: B to FF family planning sign 2000s.jpg

Label: C to EE
Description: In Chainpur, signs of agricultural activity are seldom far out of sight.  Goats feed while a motorcycle roars past.  An orange-painted mandir (“temple”) stands across the street from a white-washed masjid (“mosque”).

Label: See the muezzin make the call to prayer
Description: A muezzin (one who makes the azan) in another Chainpur mosque would make the azan (call to prayer; Arabic: adhan) using an electrified loudspeaker perched atop the minar five times daily, as has been Sunni Islamic custom.
Source Object: C to EE azan in Marai? masjid 2000s.jpg

Label: Visit the masjid
Description: One of Chainpur’s mosques can be found in the busy main bazaar.  The mosque was associated with the Deobandi movement while others were Barelvi.  Typical for much of north India, only men pray in Chainpur’s mosques while women, and many men, do so at home.
Source Object: C to EE Bazaar masjid front EDIT 2000s.jpg

Label: Enter the prayer space
Description: As one entered into the masjid, one would pass a handpump installed to aid those washing before going to namaz (daily prayers).  To the right of the door, a paper listed the different prayer times, which change over the course of a week due to changes in sunrise and sunset.
Source Object: C to EE Bazaar masjid frontal interior 2000s.jpg

Label: View the length of the prayer area
Description: The antechamber that precedes the innermost interior of the masjid (mosque) serves also as a prayer space, as evident by the woven mats laid on the floor in preparation for devotees placing their prayer rugs on top.  Seats to perform ritual washing before prayers stood at left.
Source Object: C to EE Bazaar masjid long interior w wudu seats 2000s.jpg

Label: View a minar (minaret)
Description: Minars (prayer towers) commonly have accompanied masjids in South Asia even when only decorative as here.  Originally intended centuries ago as heights from which the muezzin makes the call to prayer (azan), minars have become less important with the advent of loudspeakers (although sometimes these are placed in the minar).
Source Object: C to EE Bazaar masjid minar n steps 2000s

Label: Look to the right
Description: The shelves to the let hold copies of the Quran for anyone’s use while the empty shelves on the right wait to receive the shoes of those entering the mosque to pray.  Hindus also remove their shoes when entering temples while devotees of all religious belongings go barefoot or in socks when approaching a Sufi tomb.
Source Object: C to EE Bazaar masjid oblong interior w prayer area 2000s.jpg

Label: See where wuzu was done
Description: Wuzu (Arabic: wudu) involved the ritual washing of feet, hands, and face before namaz (daily prayers).  Prayer goers have perched pitchers above the trough to use.
Source Object: C to EE Bazaar masjid wudu seats 2000s.tif

Label: View the front of the mandir
Description: Although small, this temple has followed a common north Indian pattern of a porch-like entrance (mandapa) preceding the main, mountain-shaped garbhagriha in which the central deity has resided.

Label: See the linga and yoni
Description: The linga and the yoni in which it has for centuries represented Shiv and Devi, and their union.  Nandi the bull has been Shiv’s loyal devotee while above a bell has hung for the use of devotees who announce their presence when entering.
Source Object: C to EE mandir entrance to garbagriha 2000s

Label: View other murtis (statues)
Description: On the wall beyond the the Shiv linga and the yoni has stood murtis (statues) of other deities such as Ganesh and Hanuman.  A small stand to the right held burnt incense sticks lit by devotee as an act of veneration.
Source Object: C to EE mandir garbagriha detail 2000s

Label: Visit the Shiv mandir (“temple”)
Description: This small Shiv mandir has stood nearly opposite a masjid and has demonstrated common features to the area’s other temples.

Label: C to GG
Description: A man watches a photographer while standing on the brick-paved but potholed road to Chainpur’s Chowk Bazaar wearing a sports shirt and pants.  In the distance, another man wears a lungi wrapped around his hips and reaching his ankles as well as a scarf-like strip of cloth around his shoulders is a gamcha, the telltale piece of apparel that comes in various colors and indicates a Bihari man who works as a farmer.

Label: See Amir work
Description: Amir must first chop the tobacco into small bits, then wrap them into a tobacco leaf, before tying it tightly so it will not unwind.  When lit, biris produce a pungent, unfiltered smoke favored particularly by those who can’t afford cigarettes.

Label: See biris being made
Description: Amir, a biri maker, works all day, perhaps earning 25 rupees if he can make as many as one thousand by rolling chopped tobacco into a leaf.

Label: Read an advertisement for services offered by a family of pujaris (ritual specialists)
Description: Opposite advertisements for telecom services they offer (“STD” (Subscriber Trunk Dialing) “ISD” (International Direct Dialing) “PCO” (Public Call Office) the advertisement offers that “This is a beautiful and clean place for pilgrims to stay. Every facility is here.”
Parent: Visit a purohit (ritual specialist) serving the Harsu Brahm mandir (“temple”)
Source Object: C to GG left detail detail 2000s.jpg

Label: Visit a purohit (ritual specialist) serving the Harsu Brahm mandir (“temple”)
Description: Ramesh Tripathi sits outside his family’s home business with his brother Sitaram, awaiting those who need his services at the village’s most important mandir (“temple”) down the road.

Label: Meet a temple ritual specialist
Description: Siddharth Nath, a pujari (Hindu ritual specialist) writes his devotion across his house, with the names “Radhakrishna” and “Sitaram” painted repeatedly under the roof’s eaves and “Ram” painted in the small alcove in the wall.  He wears a gamcha a scarf particular to Bihari men slung over his shoulder.

Label: See a Bollywood film poster
Description: Among the vast array of characters in the epic Ramayan found in Sanskrit, Hindi, and other languages, Ravan has stood out in many as the arch-rival of Ram, avatar of Vishnu.  This poster advertises a Hindi-language film that showed in a Bhabhua theater with a modern Ravan as its central figure.
Source Object: C to GG Ravan film poster 2000s

Label: C to V
Description: Heading east from this intersection leads one past a corner chai dukhan (“tea shop”) and down this paved road to the muhalla (“neighborhood”) of Sonahtiya.  A child clutches a kite prepared to fly.

Label: D to AA
Description: A crowd gathered as two foreign ethnographers sought to make images of Chowk, the intersection of not only the two busiest bazaars but also the three main routes into Chainpur.

Label: Look across Chainpur from above
Description: From atop the fort’s gate, the double line of buildings comprising the bazaar led north beyond Chainpur.  The spire of a temple dominated the view at right.
Source Object: D to AA view from gate top 1990s.jpg

Label: D to E
Description: The entrance to the qila (fort) from which a raja (ruler) was said to have reigned over the area until an injustice he committed against his Brahman vizier (senior advisor) led the man to commit suicide.  Harsu Pandey thus became Harsu Brahm, a vengeful ghost who destroyed the raja and most of his family.

Label: Stay at a guest house
Description: This resthouse provided housing for pilgrims to Shastri Brahm dham.  One family has parked their truck here and proceeded on foot to the temple to make their offerings
Source Object: D to E guest house at Harsu Brahm dham 2000s.jpg

Label: Read the guest house sign
Description: “Honored Harsu Brahm Official Religious Resthouse” “Chainpur Kaimur” “A place to stay for pilgrims” “Fee: 2 rupees per pilgrim.”
Source Object: D to E guest house sign at Harsu Brahm dham 2000s.jpg

Label: Buy a history of Harsu Brahm
Description: The author of the Harsu Brahm Prakash (The Light of Harsu Brahm) produced this Hindi-language pamphlet to narrate the life of Harsu Pandey, his service and conflict with Raja Salivahan, his death by dharna (self-starvation), and return as a brahm (powerful ghost of a Brahman) worthy of worship.
Source Object: D to E Harsu Brahm Prakash for sale EDIT 2000s.jpg

Label: Buy incense
Description: The merchant offered plentiful dashang, the special incense to be burned at the abode of Harsu Brahm.
Source Object: D to E material for Harsu Brahm puja for sale 2000s.jpg

Label: Visit a shop selling pamphlets and pictures
Description: Images, narratives, and prayers all play important roles in many forms of Hindu worship.  This shop has catered to all three with framed images of the deities, printed materials describing important events involving them, and pamphlets providing prayers meant to be recited aloud during puja.
Source Object: D to E other shop and material for Harsu Brahm puja for sale 2000s.jpg

Label: Buy a devotional pamphlet
Description: Among the pamphlets for sale were narratives about Durga, Hanuman, among other deities as well as one with patriotic Indian songs.
Source Object: D to E other shop and material for Harsu Brahm puja for sale CLOSE 2000s.jpg

Label: View of shop selling ritual items
Description: Wooden sandals and coconuts, bound in colored cloth, have represented important ritual offerings to Harsu Brahm.
Source Object: D to E shop containing items from 0466 to 0468 2000s.jpg

Label: See trilingual doctor’s sign
Description: Dr. Shah Ali offered his services in English, Hindi (left), and Urdu (right), the three languages of education in Chainpur and for much of north India.  English took its script from Latin, Hindi from Sanskrit, and Urdu from Arabic and Persian.  However, most Chainpur residents have long spoken Bhojpuri as their mother language.
Source Object: D to G Dr Ali's multilingual sign 2000s.jpg

Label: D to G
Description: Although the southern end of the Chowk to bus stand road hosted Chainpur’s busiest bazaar, the road leading west from Chowk to the village Naughara also bustled with business.

Label: See building types
Description: For a village of about 8000 residents in 2001, Chainpur hosted a variety of building types.  Builders have prepared on the right a neat pile of bricks to construct a building like that behind.  Neighboring that building is a mud-plastered home or business with a terracotta-tiled roof.  In the background rises the onion-shaped dome of a Sufi’s dargah (tomb).

Label: Get student coaching
Description: Ahmad Ansari has written his name in Hindi beneath the English-language advertisement for his student coaching business, demonstrating again the rising importance and business of education.  The neighboring business offered tents for weddings and other celebrations.
Source Object: D to G Modern Guidance Coaching Centre 2000s.JPG

Label: Read an Urdu sign
Description: “Usmania Book Depot.”  Above this, from top to bottom, is “Allah,” the auspicious number “786,” and the number “92.”  Urdu uses the same numeral system as Arabic, which is related to the “Arabic numerals” used by European-language writers.
Source Object: D to G Ushmania book depot sign 2000s

Label: Visit a Yunani doctor
Description: Dr. Khan has practiced Yunani medicine, a system of health care that originated with ancient Greek knowledge (“Yunani” is Arabic for “Greek”) and was adopted and improved upon by centuries of Muslim physicians.  It has continued to be practiced in India and elsewhere into the 21st century.

Label: D to Sherpur
Description: This road leads to Sherpur, one of the smaller villages that surround Chainpur.  Residents frequently called this village constellation simply as “Chainpur” to outsiders.  Schools have just let out and sox children in private schools walk home in their uniforms while those in government schools do so in everyday wear.

Label: DD to N
Description: Empty lots in the village have provided places for chickens and goats to feed as they wander from their owners’ homes, returning in the evening to regular meals.

Label: E
Description: The Harsu Brahm Dham (abode) has capped the top of the qila (fort), demonstrating the victory of a Brahman’s vengeful ghost over Raja (ruler) Salivahan whom he once served as vizier (advisor).  Although the temple’s precincts have enclosed a large space within its white walls, its steeple did not appear very prominently.  In front of it has stood the ochre-painted Shiv temple and a metal-roofed havan (fire sacrifice place).

Label: Visit the Harsu Brahm Dham (Abode])
Description: Perhaps the young person here awaited family members who have respectfully removed their sandals before entering Harsu Brahm Dham.  The temple’s designers have established a Ganesh murti (material form) above the entranceway and the auspicious syllable Aum (or Om) above that.

Label: See the dham’s courtyard
Description: Often a crowd would fill the courtyard of the dham, small groups of family members awaiting their turn to interact with the deity as mediated through a purohit (sacrifier).

Label: View memorials left by devotees
Description: The memorials have born witness to the satisfaction which a visit to Harsu Brahm Dham has prompted for many devotees and pilgrims.  These were of four types.  The first was an inscribed stone recording the devotee's name. The second was a pinda (mound) usually of stone.  Third was a murti (material expression) of Shiv, with whom the brahm sometimes has been associated, which takes the shape of an image, linga, or symbol.  Finally, and very uncommonly, someone may have a statue of them placed so as to suggest their constant devotional presence. The red box accepted donations for the maintenance of the dham.
Source Object: E Harsu Brahm Dham courtyard details 2000s.jpg

Label: See devotees doing puja
Description: Three large festivals occur at Harsu Brahm Dham every year during which pilgrims stream from buses and private vehicles as well as on foot into the crowded courtyard to spend time in his presence, sitting in the courtyard facing his murti (material form).  During the birthday celebration of Shastri Brahm, a descendent of Harsu Brahm's personal purohit arrives an officiates at a service important for many Chainpur area residents.
Source Object: E Harsu Brahm Dham devotees sit 2000s.jpg

Label: Enter the dham
Description: Devotees customarily ring a bell when entering temples to call the attention of the deity.  Beyond the archway to the right was the firepit used to burn the offerings made to Harsu Brahm.  Ahead was the interior of the dham that houses the murti (material expression) of Harsu Brahm.  The temple courtyard stood to the left.  Because turning one’s back to a murti would be disrespectful to the deity, devotees would exit the temple by moving backwards.

Label: See the havan
Description: The havan has served as a specially designed pit where Brahmanic fire sacrifices have been made.  Vedic fire sacrifice dates to at least three thousand years ago. Fire, personified as the god Agni, has been considered by many Hindus since ancient times to be the carrier of devotions to the deities.
Source Object: E Harsu Brahm Dham havan path BEST 2000s.jpg

Label: See Harsu Brahm’s murti
Description: Harsu Brahm’s murti (material form) is a stone.  He took this form after his unjust death when he returned to Chainpur’s qila as a brahm (vengeful Brahman ghost).  This murti provides a focus for the devotee's attentions when in the temple.  The Brahman here acted as a purohit (sacrifier), the person qualified to perform the ritual, for a patron.  Because the patron actually would take responsibility for the financial and other costs of the ritual and would gain the merit from the action, they would be the sacrificer.
Source Object: E Harsu Brahm Dham murti sthan 2000s.jpg

Label: In keeping with the RSS’s Hindu nationalism, each school day began with children reciting prayers facing this altar with its garlanded images of the auspicious syllable Aum (or Om) and of Ma Bharat (Mother India), which conflated the devi’s person with the territory of India.  Between them the teachers placed an image of Harsu Brahm’s murti.
Source Object: E Harsu Brahm Saraswati Shishu Mandir altar 2000s.jpg

Label: Visit an RSS school
Description: The elementary school’s teachers have stood in the courtyard of this school established in the 2000s along principles of the Hindu nationalist organization the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (National Volunteer Society or RSS).
Source Object: E Harsu Brahm Saraswati Shishu Mandir entrance 2000s.jpg

Label: E to D
Description: The southeast corner of the temple demonstrates the success of the dham (abode).  Devotees have installed a variety of small shrines, pindas (mounds), and lingas (phallic stones) as expressions of thanks for the intervention of Harsu Brahm in the troubles of their lives.

Label: See a closeup of a linga and saptmatrika
Description: Devotees of Harsu Brahm have installed this linga (murti stone) devoted to the god Shiv in the foreground. Behind it is the saptmatrika (seven mothers) dedicated to seven goddesses.

Label: See the southern edge of Chainpur
Description: Chainpur’s southern habitations effectively end at the fort with mostly its fields stretching beyond.  In the dim distance is the start of the Kaimur Hills, which are part of the northern edge of India’s central Deccan Plateau.

Label: See a sap tapper
Description: Some village residents would climb a palm tree to tap its sap in order to make toddy, a folk alcoholic drink that became illegal.
Source Object: E to south climbing tree for toddy 1990s.jpg

Label: View a village and it fields
Description: The trees of this small village between Chainpur and the towering cliffs of the Kaimur Hills have offered shade and products (like coconuts and sap for toddy) to the residents when they have taken a break from working their fields.  The crop would be harvested after some months.

Label: See water buffalo
Description: Water buffalo have provided crucial resources of milk and labor.  These have returned from time wallowing in a pond or tank.

Label: EE to C
Description: A boy has taken a pushcart past a Jeep parked by an Islamic masjid (mosque) and a Hindu mandir (temple) that have long stood opposite one another.

Label: Buy fruit from a pushcart
Description: Pushcarts have offered merchants the mobility to sell fruits, vegetables, or other goods along every street and gali (alley) in the village.
Source Object: EE to C cart in Chowk Bazaar from above 2000s.jpg

Label: Visit a medicine shop
Description: Suresh Choudhari completed his studies at Banaras Hindu University (BHU) and returned home to Chainpur to open this medical store.  Surrounded by shelves full of medicines, he has hung above where he sat a portrait of Chandrashekhar Azad, an Indian freedom fighter who died in 1931 while leading armed resistance against British rule in the previous years.
Source Object: EE to C Choudhari Medical Hall 2000s.jpg

Label: Read the store’s sign
Description: “Choudhari Medical Hall” “Chainpur, Kaimur-Bhabhua” “Note English, Ayurvedic, and homeopathic veterinary medicines also can be found here.”
Source Object: EE to C Choudhari Medical Hall sign 2000s.jpg

Label: Meet the chai dukhan’s customers
Description: The presence of Imran Khan, Vijay Singh, M. Adil Khan, and Vikesh Singh among Balu’s customers reflects how Hindus and Muslims and even sometimes Sikhs commonly share one another’s company in such social spaces.
Parent: A great deal of Chainpur’s socializing centers on chai (tea).  Hosts
Source Object: EE to C corner chai dukhan customers 2000s.jpg

Label: A great deal of Chainpur’s socializing centers on chai (tea).  Hosts
Description: other than some who can’t afford it routinely serve chai to visitors to their homes.  In public spaces, chai dukhans (shops) prove central gathering places for communing, conversation, news, and gossip.  Balu keeps busy ensuring that the chai is piping hot and the snacks are freshly made.
Source Object: EE to C corner chai dukhandar 2000s.jpg

Label: EE to FF
Description: The road to Chowk Bazaar passed a one of each of Chainpur’s many mandirs (“temples”) and masjids (“mosques”).

Label: See a family store
Description: The Agrawal family has run this shop for decades.  Earlier, they only developed photographic film and made photocopies, representing the only local business to do so.  But in the 1990s, the Agrawals added the first international telephone booth in Chainpur.

Label: Enter Agrawal studio
Description: Sanjit Agrawal offers much more than film, photocopying, and telephone services.  He also makes identification photos, takes family photos, and sells devotional items.  The top shelf holds framed portraits of (from right to left) Mohandas (“Mahatma”) Gandhi, K.S. Hedgewar (founder of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh or RSS), and M.S. Golwalker (second leader of the RSS).
Source Object: EE to FF Agrawal Studio inside 2000s.jpg

Label: Use the store’s telecommunications
Description: “STD (Subscriber Trunk Dialing)” “ISD (International Direct Dialing)” “PCO (Public Call Office)” [These three services provided, respectively, national, international, and local telephone calling] “National and international specific telephone service and telephone [remainder obscured by poster]”
Source Object: EE to FF Agrawal Studio ISD STD PCO sign 2000s.jpg

Label: Buy a devotional item
Description: Alongside shelves with images of the Islamic figure Buraq (lower left) and the Hindu Devi (center left), stood those (upper left) with images of Durga, Hanuman, Kali, and the local Harsu Brahm as well as murtis (statues) of Lakshmi and Ganesh used by these like other Hindu storeowners for daily puja.  Below this stood an image of B.R. Ambedkar, the freedom fighter who authored India’s Constitution and led the Dalit (“crushed”) movement.
Source Object: EE to FF Agrawal Studio items 2000s.jpg

Label: Read the store’s main sign
Description: “Agrawal Studios – artist and photographer” “Chainpur, Kaimur (Bhabhua) district” “Our store can make black & white and color photos beautiful and clean” “Our store is a photographic service for weddings and preparations” “Photo framing available here.”
Source Object: EE to FF Agrawal Studio sign 2000s.jpg

Description: Muhammad Adil has sat at his pedal-powered sewing machine, able to tailor even during the frequent failures of the electrical supply.  He wore a lungi (waist cloth) to keep cool in the heat.
Source Object: EE to FF Dehati Kurta Tailors 2000s.jpg

Label: Read the tailor shop’s sign
Description: “Village Kurta Tailor Master” in Hindi.
Source Object: EE to FF Dehati Kurta Tailors sign 2000s.jpg

Label: See a sign for an Islamic school
Description: The sign advertised an Islamic elementary school (maktab) where children learn Quranic reading and recitation, among other schools.  It stands behind the buildings seen here.

Label: See locally made fuel
Description: These dried patties were made from a mixture of straw and gobar (“cow dung”).  Although their smoke when burned in homes proved unhealthy, they have remained an inexpensive fuel source for those who cannot afford electricity or natural gas.  Each bore the hand print of its maker.
Source Object: EE to FF west dried gobar 2000s.jpg

Label: FF to B
Description: The corner of a mud-plastered, stone-walled home has collapsed on the left, necessitating repairs.  Newer homes and businesses increasingly have relied on brick, as seen with the surrounding buildings.  Although the road has been paved, accumulated wear and earth causes muddy puddles to form after rainstorms.

Label: FF to EE
Description: As some residents stared at the foreign ethnographer photographing the scene, others passed the increasingly dense group of shops that constitute Chainpur’s main bazaar as they walk the main road toward the intersection known as Chowk.

Label: G to D
Description: Electrical lines has long brought current to many Chainpur homes, although perhaps only for a few hours per day if at all some weeks.

Label: G to K
Description: Children frequently run to the bazaar on an errand for a parent or other family member.

Label: See Chainpur’s congregational mosque
Description: Although a Sunni Muslim community may use many mosques in its vicinity, most male members would gather for the special Friday noon prayer at the Jama Masjid (congregational mosque).
Source Object: G to K and G to M Jama Masjid 2000s.tif

Label: See a namaz position
Description: One of the many prayer positions in namaz is prostration, an act of ultimate submission to Allah.  Only men pray at the mosques in Chainpur.  Women do their prayers at home, as do many men unless it is the Friday noon prayer.
Source Object: G to K and G to M Jama Masjid prostration 1990s.jpg

Label: See Muslims perform wuzu
Description: These seats allow Muslims to wash their face, head, ears, mouth, nostrils, hands, arms, feet, and ankles in the manner prescribed as wuzu (Arabic: wudu) before doing the formal, ritual prayer of namaz (Arabic: salat). These ablutions ensure a properly purified condition before undertaking prayers to Allah.
Source Object: G to K and G to M Jama Masjid wuzu 2000s .jpg

Label: Visit the Elephant Well (or is it the Hand Well?)
Description: Between the Jama Masjid and the road, this stepwell has existed for centuries.  Some residents call it “Hath Kua” and claim it is a “hand well” for Muslims to do wuzu (ceremonial cleansing) before namaz (regular prayers) at the neighboring Jama Masjid.  Others say that because the local raja built this to wash his elephant, its name is “Hathi Kua.”  The Hindi and Urdu word Hathi derives from hath since elephants can use the end of their trunks like a hand.

Label: Choose your medicine
Description: Although Prabunath’s family business Sri Mahadev Medical, as written on the rooftop sign has focused on homeopathic medicine, he also has sold allopathic and ayurvedic medicines.  Three generations of his family have run this shop.

Label: Enter the store
Description: Prabunath and his brother staff the counter, sometimes recommending treatments as well as selling medicines prescribed by doctors.  The store’s success had been enough for Prabunath to quit his teaching job and open a new shop in Chainpur’s bazaar.
Source Object: G to K Nandlal's store counter 2000s.jpg

Label: See Prabunath get interviewed
Description: An American ethnographer interviewed Prabunath about his life and business in Chainpur.
Source Object: G to K Nandlal’s store Prem interviews Nandlal 2000s.jpg

Label: Read the store’s sign
Description: The store’s sign was sponsored by “Him Jewels” which, according to the text at top, was “Made from Himalayan herbs” and an “Ayurvedic soft oil.”  As to the store, the sign declared at right that “Here is the sole seller of English [i.e., Western or allopathic], Yunani, Ayurvedic, and herbal medicine.” “English” referenced Western or allopathic medicine; “Yunani” referenced “Greek” medicine that medieval Arab physicians developed as a system; and “Ayurvedic” medicine originated in ancient South Asia.
Source Object: G to K Nandlal's store sign 2000s.jpg

Label: G to M
Description: A devotee enters a Sufi mazar (tomb) from this pathway.

Label: Visit the Sufi tomb of Mubarak Shah
Description: Certainly, one of the most important religious sites in Chainpur has been the tomb of Mubarak Shah.  Tended by the descendants of this ascetic Muslim intellectual, the onion-domed tomb has stood at the corner of the village's large Jama Masjid (congregational mosque).  Devotees, Hindu and Muslim, frequent this site throughout the year, offering prayers and making requests.

Label: See inside the Sufi’s tomb
Description: With a gravestone at its head and a money box for donations at its foot, the tomb of the Sufi was covered in chadars (cloth sheets) and strings of flowers left by devotees. These devotees celebrated Mubarak Shah's urs (death day celebrations) on the 13th of Jumadas-sani in the Islamic calendar, coming even from neighboring states.  On another night, a pair of dueling qawwali musical troupes would match wits until near dawn in a field behind the fort with an audience of hundreds of nexus dwellers.
Source Object: G to M left detail horizontal 2000s.jpg

Label: See the performance of dua
Description: While Muslims perform namaz (salat) at specified times of the day such as before dawn, noon, and at sunset, they perform the prayer form of dua at any time they consider it appropriate to supplicate God, cupping their hands together and addressing Allah.

Label: Enter a barber shop
Description: Faisal Yacqub sits in front of his barber shop under the shade of a thatched roof.  His shop bears the marks of public health measures such as the record of an application of the pesticide DDT to the right of the door and the handwritten adage on the wall around the corner “India made this pledge: To eliminate leprosy.”  Leprosy victims in the Chainpur area don’t face the stigma found in other places in India, expediting their cure.

Label: Get a haircut
Description: Faisal Yacqub stands in his barber shop awaiting a customer.
Source Object: GG to AA barber shop inside 2000s.jpg

Label: See Bollywood’s influence
Description: “Bharat Tailors” took its name from another name for India. The sign above the tailor featured the famous Hindi-language film actor Amitabh Bachchan standing with a woman by a mountain lake.  Hindi films play throughout the world and Mumbai (formerly Bombay), the center of India's film industry, produces more movies than any other city in the world.  Hence the term “Bollywood.”  Chainpur residents had to go to Bhabhua, twenty kilometers away, to see a movie in a theater.  Only a few wealthy residents watched videos on televisions.

Label: Read the sign
Description: “Bharat Tailors.” “Ladies and gents, baggy pants, suit specialist,” “Chainpur Kaimur (Bhabhua).”  Perhaps the tailor hopes to cater to the Bhojpuri-language film industry.
Source Object: GG to AA Bharat Tailors sign 2000s.jpg

Label: GG to AA
Description: The closer to Chowk Bazaar, the denser the businesses become.  Stores for cloth, readymade clothing, paan, and home goods are all on display for those passing by.

Label: Daily, Lacchan Das sets up his shoe business mending shoes of leather and plastic in the unused space adjacent to Faisal Yacqub’s barber shop with whom he commonly can be found in casual conversation when not tending to customers.
Visit a paan shop
Description: Vyas Chaurasiya runs one of the several paan shops in Chainpur.  His shop also sells various plastic- and foil-wrapped treats but his speciality is preparing paan. The swastika above his head indicates auspiciousness and continues the use of an Indian symbol dating from ancient times. NO LINK!

Label: Vyas folds the paan
Description: After chuna, katha, betel nut, and tobacco are applied—the paan is expertly folded so it can slide easily into the consumer’s mouth. NO LINK!
Source Object: GG to AA paan wala folds 2000s.jpg

Label: Learn about the wonders of paan
Description: Consisting of betel nut wrapped in a leaf along with other ingredients, paan has been a delicacy in north India for centuries, once served in the courts of royalty. Betel causes a mild effect for the chewer while other ingredients including coconut, tobacco, or cardamom can be added.  The shops of well-respected pan walas become destinations in their own right. NO LINK!
Source Object: GG to AA paan wala table 2000s.jpg

Label: GG to C
Description: Wearing a green sari with an orange bodice, this woman is one of the relative few walking through the bazaar.  Chainpur’s public spaces tended to be used by men with women of higher status economic status often restricted to home as an expression of that status.  Women who worked outside could not be held within such limits.

Label: K to G
Description: The bazaar extending to Chowk Bazaar from the westward road begins here.

Label: K to L
Description: This gali (alley) leads to the neighborhoods of Jama Masjid and Marai.

Label: K to Naughara
Description: Chainpur’s roads have had to bear the burden of foot traffic, especially pedestrians laden with crops and possessions, and vehicles varying from bicycle rickshaws carrying passengers to trucks transporting heavy cargoes.  Along this road, businesses and residences tapered off into fields before entering the neighboring village of Naughara.

Label: See a college bus
Description: In the 2000s, a nearby college offered students from the village of Naughara daily transportation to its classrooms.  This provided yet another indication of the rising importance of tertiary education for a growing middle class.

Label: View an Indian roller
Description: Indian rollers flash their bright colors while in flight across north India.  Their Hindi name, Neelkanth (Blue-throated), references an instance in a Hindu narrative of cosmic creation.  As the primordial cosmic ocean churned, a poison emerged that the god Shiv swallowed in order to protect the nascent world.  Held in his throat, the poison turned it blue, and so “Neelkanth” became one of the deity’s names.

Label: L to K
Description: A few Muslim tombs stood along the land behind the Jama Masjid and alongside the gali (alley) leading to the Chowk to Naughara road.

Label: L to M
Description: The carefully-patterned brick pavement of this street afforded easier travel by foot, bicycle, scooter, motorcycle, or seldomly car.

Label: M to BB
Description: The road leads from muhallas (neighborhoods) of Marai and Jama Masjid to Chowk Bazaar.

Label: M to G
Description: This street passes in front of the very expensive house on the left, built by a family who had a member working overseas for two decades.

Label: Visit a masjid
Description: Following the street westward from Jama Masjid, one would come across the Marai muhalla (neighborhood) that included this masjid (mosque).  As was common throughout much of South Asia, this masjid’s aesthetic attraction rests on it various architectural members (such as the notional minars (towers for calling to prayer)), floral patterns, geometric design, and calligraphy.
Source Object: M to L Marai? masjid beautification 2000s.jpg

Label: See calligraphy applied
Description: This painter works to complete the calligraphy above the entrance gate to the newly repainted masjid.  He carefully drew temporary horizontal lines to ensure that he properly renders each Arabic letter as conjoined with others to form the flowing beauty of every word.
Source Object: M to L Marai? masjid beautification CLOSE 2000s.jpg

Label: M to L DETAIL
Description: This street leaves Jama Masjid and heads to Marai.  Households that could afford to do so had water pumped into large plastic water tanks on their roofs to ensure access to water in case of electrical outage, which might happen for many hours a day, or even for the full day.

Label: M to N
Description: This gali (“alley”) leads to a neighborhood with three homes once owned by three brothers.

Label: N to DD
Description: This trail leaves the small neighborhood in which the Sayyid family lives and heads north into other muhallas.

Label: N to M
Description: The concrete-covered brick buildings and well paved gali (alley) evidence the relative wealth in this part of Chainpur.

Label: Buy medicine
Description: Suresh Choudhari completed his studies at Banaras Hindu University (BHU) and returned home to Chainpur to open a medical store. Recently he moved the store from farther down the road toward Chowk where it stood in the 2000s.
Source Object: A to B Choudhari Medical Hall 2020s.jpg

Label: Watch a Kingfisher take flight
Description: A White-throated kingfisher launches from its wire perch near the tank that offers a birds-eye view of potential fish meals in the waters below.

Label: Watch a raptor eat
Description: This raptor, known as a Shikar, enjoys a mouse as a meal.
Source Object: A to Bhabua shikar feeding in tree best.JPG

Label: A to Jagariya
Description: These e-scooters or e-rickshaws vie with rickshaws for passengers to Jagariya and other villages to the north of the bus stand. While some motor rickshaws use natural gas, those burning gasoline use highly polluting two-stroke engines. Meanwhile, a massive highway will soon stretch from east to west ten kilometers or so in this direction offering yet more motorized connectivity to Banaras and to the rest of Bihar and north India.
Source Object: A to Jagariya line of E-Scooters.jpg

Label: See a Babbler
Description: The Babbler, known as Chocha locally, can be found around gardens and clearings.
Source Object: AA to BB Babbler (chocha) on wall.JPG

Description: Empty cages stand near a basket of beheaded chickens. Chainpur consumers of meat often see their meals at the first stage of their preparation.

Description: A couple of businesses line the first few meters of this street leading from Chowk Bazaar before giving way to residences.

Description: A group of friends with diverse religious backgrounds, most of whom met in high school, and including a foreign ethnographer have long made this store their social center.

Description: Ustad and Yahya prepare to go to mosques for namaz (“regular prayer”) during Ramzan (or Ramadan), the month when Muslims celebrate the first revelation of the Quran. Although Ustad regularly covers his head for Islamic reasons, Yahya only does for this month.
Parent: Visit a cloth store and social place
Source Object: AA to D Shyam Babu's store Ramzan gear.JPG

Label: AA to D
Description: The north-south road from the bus stand terminates in Chowk Bazaar. Chowk refers to a habitation’s major intersection. In Chainpur, the road from the north intersects not only with the most important road leading east and west but also the entrance to the qila (“fort”) where the busiest Hindu temple stands. That entrance begins under the large orange arch seen at the road’s end.

Label: See Islamic decorations
Description: A clockface chalked on this store’s door helps advertise the business of Golden Watch. The Islamic symbol of a crescent moon with star hangs above a similarly chalked image of the Taj Mahal in Agra. The artist includes a view of the garden in which this most iconic of Indian buildings stands. Meanwhile, the Arabic numbers above the door (“786”) represent the Islamic system of abjad that assigns letters in words to numbers as a form of religious arithmetic. 786 is particularly auspicious.
Source Object: B to FF (r) Taj on door.JPG

Label: B to FF
Description: A view of the road leading to Chowk in Chainpur from the bus stand. This is the northern edge of Chainpur’s habitations and businesses.

Label: See a political candidate’s poster
Description: The poster by this political candidate for Chainpur’s panchayat (village counsel) congratulates those celebrating the Hindu holidays of Dashara, Dhanteras, Diwali, and Dala Chat Puja.
Source Object: B to FF candidate posters inside.JPG

Label: See posters on a building
Description: Multiple candidates have posted their advertisements here.

Description: This well-paved street with a deep run-off channel replaced the dirt street that existed thirty years ago. This makes passage much less muddy and challenging during the annual monsoon when rain barrages commonly fall. DELETE

Description: In his basket, the pujari brings raisins for prasad (gifts to and from deities), a bell for drawing the deity’s attention, a brass lota (“water vessel”) for pouring libations, and red- and yellow-colored thread for tying protective rakshasutra bracelets around devotee wrists following the puja.

The white scarf-like strip of cloth around his shoulders is a gamcha, the telltale piece of apparel that comes in various colors and indicates a Bihari man who works as a farmer.

Description: Discarded plastic packaging litters most village spaces not occupied by habitations, businesses, or cultivated fields. Without any regular trash collection service, the village has few options.

Description: Two-wheeled transport offers an option that proves less expensive than cars which most cannot afford and are better able to negotiate sometimes thick traffic and/or narrow roads.

Description: Children frequently run errands in the bazaar for their families. Perhaps a guest requires chilled, bottled water, if that’s affordable to the family. Before the 2020s, shops around Chainpur did not carry bottled drinks, let alone refrigerated ones.

Label: D to Sherpur
Description: This road leads to Sherpur, one of the smaller villages that surround Chainpur. These represent a constellation of villages that residents reference as a whole to outsiders by using the name of its social, economic, and religious center: “Chainpur.” Handcarts provide help moving merchandise when a motor vehicle isn’t available or affordable.

Label: See a pilgrim’s car
Description: The plates on this car suggest that it came from Uttar Pradesh, the state neighboring Bihar to the west. This indicates how broadly devotion to Harsu Brahm has spread. Meanwhile, the poster behind advertises the services of a purohit (ritual specialist) who serves the brahm’s mandir (“temple”). Toys and games stand alongside malas (“flower necklaces”) and decorated cloths used as gifts to the deity propitiated by the devotee.
Source Object: E detail pilgrims from UP EDIT.JPG

Label: See an egret complain
Description: Well, it’s not really complaining: it just might look that way. The egret might be managing the heat by breathing with its beak open.

Label: Visit the Harsu Brahm Dham [“Abode”]
Description: As some devotees exit carrying the platter with which they brought their offerings, others piously enter Harsu Brahm Dham by touching the threshold with their right hand before touching their head as a sign of respect.

Label: See ceiling beautification
Description: Over the decades, the dham has been expanded and beautified: even the mounts for the fans that prove so necessary in the summer months.
Source Object: E Harsu Brahm Dham ceiling design.JPG

Label: See a devotee’s anjali
Description: Bowing his head, a devotee makes the reverential motion of an anjali mudra (“anjali hand position”) toward the brahm’s murti (material form), pressing his hands together.
Source Object: E Harsu Brahm Dham devotee anjali.JPG

Label: See devotees sitting
Description: As some devotees make their way to receive darshan (“being seen”) from Harsu Brahm, others spend more time in his presence, sitting in the courtyard facing his murti (material form).
Source Object: E Harsu Brahm Dham devotees sit.JPG

Label: See the way to the havan
Description: These devotees exit toward the havan, a specially designed pit where brahmanic fire sacrifices are made. Vedic fire sacrifice dates to three thousand years ago.
Source Object: E Harsu Brahm Dham havan path BEST.JPG

Label: See Harsu Brahm’s murti
Description: Harsu Brahm’s murti (material form) is a stone. He took this form after his unjust death when he returned to Chainpur’s qila as an angry Brahman ghost, or brahm.
Source Object: E Harsu Brahm Dham murti sthan.JPG

Label: See the stairs to another temple
Description: A second and then a third floor were added to the dham (“abode”) since 2000, with a temple to the goddess Durga as well.
Source Object: E Harsu Brahm Dham stairs up.JPG

Label: E
Description: The Harsu Brahm Dham (“Abode”) dominates the top of the qila (“fort”), demonstrating the victory of a Brahman’s vengeful ghost over a raja (“ruler”) he once served as vizier (“advisor”). The building in front is for the havan (“fire sacrifice place”).
Source Object: E Harsu Brahm mandir over havan area.JPG

Label: D to E
Description: The entrance to the qila (“fort”) from which a raja (“ruler”) is said to have reigned over the area until an injustice he committed against his Brahman vizier (“senior advisor”) led the man to commit suicide. Harsu Pandey thus became Harsu Brahm, a vengeful ghost who destroyed the raja and most of his family.

Label: See a tractor at work
Description: Over the past decades, tractors have become more ubiquitous in Chainpur and more powerful, gradually replacing oxen and water buffalo as beasts of burden.
Parent: See the southern edge of Chainpur
Source Object: E to south farm tractor with trailer of grain 2020s.jpeg

Label: View the harvest
Description: Under the supervision of landowner Vir Singh, men and women labor to bring in the masur (lentil) harvest. Labor-intensive agricultural work still employs the majority of Chainpur area residents despite increasing mechanization.

Label: See a water tank program
Description: The state government created a scheme to increase access to fresh water that led to the construction of water towers here and elsewhere around the area.
Parent: See the southern edge of Chainpur
Source Object: E to south water tank government scheme.JPG

Label: See the southern edge of Chainpur
Description: Chainpur’s southern habitations effectively end at the fort with mostly its fields stretching beyond. In the dim distance is the start of the Kaimur Hills, which are part of the northern edge of India’s central Deccan Plateau.

Label: EE to C
Description: The road to Chowk Bazaar passes a pair of Chainpur’s many mandirs (“temples”) and masjids (“mosques”).

Label: Visit the masjid
Description: One of Chainpur’s mosques can be found in the busy main bazaar. The posters on it reflect various elements of Muslim life in the area. The mosque is associated with the Deobandi movement.

Label: See ads for a girls’ school, pilgrimage travel, and a celebration of the Prophet Muhammad’s birthday
Description: Although most Muslim women in Chainpur do not wear niqab (the covering of all of the head except for the face), this Urdu advertisement for a girls’ school shows a student wearing it. To the left, a Hindi ad for Fatima Travels offers various prices for pilgrimage packages to hajj or umra. Above this, an ad in Hindi and Urdu for a conference and celebration to take place on the eve of the Prophet Muhammad’s birthday.

Label: See an ad for an award ceremony
Description: This poster, mostly in Urdu, announces an event awarding ceremonial turbans to those involved in Islamic studies. Urdu’s script derives from Arabic and Persian orthography and can be a highly developed art form.

Label: See the proclamation of faith
Description: Above the entrance to the mosque, the Islamic proclamation of faith shahadah declares La ilaha illah Allah, Muhammadur rasul Allah (“There is one God, and Muhammad is His Prophet”).

Label: View the temple components
Description: Although small, this temple follows a common north Indian pattern of a porch-like entrance (mandapa) preceding the main, mountain-shaped garbhagriha in which the central deity resides.

Label: See the temple entrance
Description: A mantra above the mandir’s entrance exclaims “Salutation to you Sri Shiva.” The entrance gives the impression of entering a mountain.
Source Object: EE mandir Salutation to you Sri Shiva.JPG

Label: Enter the mandir
Description: Leaves adorn the entrance into the garbagriha (“inner sanctuary”), which has a Shiv linga and a murti of Nandi at center.

Label: View inside the temple
Description: The Shiv linga and the yoni in which it sits represent Shiv and Devi, and their union. Nandi the bull is Shiv’s loyal devotee while on the wall opposite them an image of the goddess Durga another expression of Devi looks back at the visitor.

Label: See a family store
Description: The Agrawal family has run this shop for more than three decades. In the 1990s, it not only developed photographic film and made photocopies, but also had the first international telephone booth in Chainpur. Technological advances have made most of these services redundant.

Label: See Chainpur’s first franchise store
Description: Oppo opened the first franchise store to appear in Chainpur. The Chinese smartphone and electronics company has had its own retail stores in India only since 2017.

Label: Visit the Shiv mandir (“temple”)
Description: This small Shiv mandir stands nearly opposite a masjid and demonstrates common features to the area’s temples.
Source Object: EE to FF Shiv mandir enter.JPG

Label: View cow dung fuel
Description: These dried patties are a mixture of straw and gobar (“cow dung”). Although their smoke when burned in homes is unhealthy, they remain an inexpensive fuel source for those who cannot afford electricity or natural gas.
Source Object: EE to FF west dried gobar.JPG

Label: Read a Cool Creators ad
Description: Cool Creators advertises a wide variety of products, including “fridges, standing closets, beds, sofas, blenders, irons, induction ovens, fans, coolers, and mobiles, etc.” Although written in Hindi and using some Hindi-origin terms, many of the words used on this ad derive from English terms taken up when the Western-originated technology was adopted by consumers.
Source Object: EE to FF west sign EDIT.jpg

Label: Watch out! Tractor!
Description: Tractors and their trailers are ubiquitous around Chainpur as farmers bring their harvests to mills and grain buyers located in and around this important area economic center.
Source Object: farm tractor with trailer of grain vertical.JPG

Label: See Chainpur’s expansion
Description: Chainpur continues to grow, especially along the road between the thana and Chainpur Chowk. New homes and businesses emerge annually.
Source Object: FF to B east Heritage Global School bus partial.JPG

Label: See a school bus for one of the local private schools
Description: Education is one of the fastest growing economic sectors in the Chainpur area, as well as in India as a whole. Parents have the choice of many more private schools and better government schools than two decades earlier.
Source Object: FF to B east Heritage Global School bus.JPG

Label: See water buffalo
Description: Water buffalo play a critical role in the agricultural economy. Not only do locals relish its milk thicker and sweeter than a cow’s but also they take its dung, form it into patties mixed with straw, and dry it in the sun. The results are evident in the background and are used to fuel kitchen fires and fires to keep those guarding fields warm at night.
Source Object: FF to B west buffalo best.JPG

Label: FF to EE
Description: A family, perhaps arriving from a bus journey, walks along Chainpur’s main road.

Label: Read a sign for a clothing shop
Description: The Hindi-language sign for this ready-made garment shop advertises “Our place has saris, shirts, dress material, and ready-made vests at appropriate prices.” Notably, the models pictured all have very fair complexions. Many Chainpur residents among many other Indians equate beauty with fairer skin complexions.

Label: Buy fish
Description: A fishmonger uses scales to weigh recently caught fish in preparation for selling them.
Source Object: G to D right detail detail.JPG

Label: See a food cart
Description: Top in Town offers various foods such as parathas, egg rolls, chicken rolls, and chicken egg rolls.
Source Object: G to D Top in Town.JPG

Label: Buy vegetables
Description: Various vegetables and melons are for sale.

Label: See changes in telecommunications
Description: Chainpur has witnessed the feverish technological changes that have swept India as a whole. New technologies like satellite dishes arrive and swiftly find competition with newer types of equipment.
Source Object: G to K abandoned satellite dishes.JPG

Label: See Chainpur’s Friday mosque
Description: Although a Muslim community may use many mosques, most members will gather for the special Friday noon prayer at the Jama Masjid (“congregational mosque”).
Source Object: G to K and G to M Jama Masjid.JPG
Note: Not in Peter's Drive under this name; Hasib will share the file

Label: G to K
Description: A man and his wife travel on their motorcycle toward Naughara or Malik Sarai, two villages to the west of Chainpur.

Label: Visit the Elephant Well (or is it the Hand Well?)
Description: Between the Jama Masjid and the road is a centuries-old stepwell. Some residents call it “Hath-i Kua” and claim it is a “hand well” for Muslims to do wuzu (ceremonial cleansing) before namaz (regular prayers) at the neighboring Jama Masjid. Others say that because the local raja built this to wash his elephant, its name is “Hathi Kua.” The Hindi and Urdu word Hathi derives from hath since elephants can use the end of their trunks like a hand.
Note: Not in Peter's Drive under this name; Hasib will share the file

Label: See a carved lotus
Description: Although fallen leaves and plastic rubbish cover the stairs of the stepwell, some architectural flourishes, such as this stone-carved lotus remain evident.
Parent: Visit the Elephant Well (or is it the Hand Well?)
Source Object: G to K Hath(i) Kua arch lotus.JPG

Label: Get medicine
Description: Although Nandlal’s business Sri Mahadev Medical Hall, as written above his head focuses on homeopathic medicine, he also sells allopathic and ayurvedic medicines. Three generations of his family have run this shop.
Note: Not in Peter's Drive under this name; Hasib will share the file

Label: See Mubarak Shah’s tomb
Description: Chainpur Muslims have built a mazar (“tomb”) for Sufi Mubarak Shah alongside the Jama Masjid, which they continue to expand.

Label: The Muslim community continues to expand the Jama Masjid, adding additional floors above and attachments alongside.
Description: The Muslim community continues to expand the Jama Masjid, adding additional floors above and attachments alongside.

Label: See the Sufi’s tomb inside
Description: With a gravestone at its head and a money box for donations at its foot, the tomb of Mubarak Shah is covered in chadars and strings of flowers left by devotees.
Source Object: G to M left detail horizontal.JPG

Label: See the decorations celebrating Mubarak Shah
Description: From an overhanging sheet, streamers of various sorts hang down in celebration of the Sufi.
Source Object: G to M left detail vertical.JPG

Label: See a corner view of the mazar
Description: The onion-dome represents one element of “Islamicate” architecture. Not all buildings built by Muslims with such a dome are religious in design, but this architectural element stems from cultures deeply informed by Islamic influences.

Label: G to M
Description: A devotee enters a Sufi mazar (“tomb”) from this pathway.

Label: See bicycle repair business
Description: east Sitaram and Raju Paswan daily set up their bicycle repair business on the curbside in front of a vegetable store. Sitaram wears a shirt and lungi (long cloth worn around his waist) while Raju wears a T-shirt, shorts, and a gamcha, the cloth wrapped around the neck or slung on the shoulder that is pervasive among rural Bihari men.
Source Object: GG to AA east Sitaram and Raju Paswan bicycle repairmen smile.JPG

Label: Visit a paan shop
Description: Rajesh Kumar Chaurasiya has run his paan shop here for decades. He is surrounded by various plastic- and foil-wrapped treats but his speciality is preparing paan.
Parent: Learn about the wonders of paan
Source Object: GG to AA Rajesh Kumar Chaurasiya paan dukhan detail detail.JPG

Label: Learn about the wonders of paan
Description: Consisting of betel nut wrapped in a leaf along with other ingredients, paan has been a delicacy in north India for centuries, once served in the courts of royalty. Betel causes a mild effect for the chewer while other ingredients including coconut, tobacco, or cardamom can be added. The shops of well-respected pan walas become destinations in their own right.
Source Object: GG to AA Rajesh Kumar Chaurasiya paan dukhan detail.JPG

Label: Read the sign
Description: The Hindi-language sign outside the shop reads “Brother Ramji, paan wala.” “Wala” means someone who does something.
Parent: Learn about the wonders of paan
Source Object: GG to AA Rajesh Kumar Chaurasiya paan dukhan enter.JPG

Label: GG to AA
Description: A school van brings children home at day’s end, reflecting one of the Chainpur area’s fastest growing sectors with increasing numbers of privately-run schools and improving government-run schools.

Label: See a non-human Chainpur resident
Description: This Green bee eater, among many other birds, makes the most out of electrical lines that allow for a hunting perch and a place of refuge from land predators.

Label: Watch Dharmendra work
Description: Dharmendra drops string beans into the fryer above an open flame.
Parent: Pappu and his brother Dhamendra have managed this chai dukhan (“tea shop”) for decades. Some consider theirs the best tea and namkeen (“fried salty snacks”) in Chainpur, while they also sell sweets like jalebis.

Label: Have some pakora
Description: Pakoras are fried vegetables while triangular samosas may be stuffed with peas or potato, then fried.
Parent: Pappu and his brother Dhamendra have managed this chai dukhan (“tea shop”) for decades. Some consider theirs the best tea and namkeen (“fried salty snacks”) in Chainpur, while they also sell sweets like jalebis.

Label: Try some namkeen
Description: Namkeen come in various sorts but are all fried salty snacks.

Label: K to Naughara
Description: The bazaar that extends from Chowk continues westward until Chainpur’s muhallas (neighborhoods) thin in density along the road to the village of Naughara. The changes in building density since the 2000s demonstrates well the growth of Chainpur from 9000 then to 11,000 residents in 2011. In comparison, Chainpur only had 3,500 residents in 1981.

Label: L to M
Description: A decade or so earlier, this rugged paved road replaced the parquet-patterned brick surfaced street just as pakka (“proper”), brick-built buildings increasingly replace kaccha (“raw”) dried-mud walled ones.

Label: M to BB
Description: The road leads from muhallas (“neighborhoods”) of Marai and Jama Masjid to Chowk Bazaar.

Label: M to G
Description: This street passes in front of the very expensive house on the left, built by a family who had a member working overseas for two decades.

Label: See posters on a home in Marai
Description: Following the street westward from Jama Masjid, one finds these posters on a home in Marai muhalla (“neighborhood”). Above a Hindi advertisement for Vim dishwashing detergent promising to remove greasiness, another poster uses English, Arabic, and Hindi as well as the heart symbol. The Arabic calligraphy at right invokes Allah while that at left depicts Muhammad’s name. At bottom, the Hindi phrase states that the English-language sentiment “I love Muhammad” is “on behalf of the muhalla Ghazi Miyan Roza [tomb], Chainpur.”
Source Object: M to L I Love Muhammad poster in Maral TWEAK BETTER.jpg

Label: M to L
Description: This street leaves Jama Masjid and heads to Marai. Households that can afford to do so have water pumped into large plastic water tanks on their roofs to ensure access to water in case of electrical outage, even though this usually only happens for a few hours daily, a vast improvement from previous decades.

Label: BB to M
Description: This road leads towards the muhalla (“neighborhood”) of Marai in which a number of Muslim families live. DELETE

Label: Visit the family masjid
Description: For untold generations, the family inhabiting this muhalla (“neighborhood”) has used this small masjid (“mosque”).
Source Object: M to N family masjid exterior oblong 2020s.JPG

Label: M to N
Description: This gali (“alley”) leads to a neighborhood with three homes once owned by three brothers and their family’s masjid (“mosque”).

Label: Enter the family masjid
Description: Sayyid Umar and his son approach the gate to the masjid’s courtyard.

Label: Enter the courtyard
Description: Mosques in South Asia commonly have two prayer areas: an outer one open to the sky and an enclosed one entered from the latter. The shelves on the left can be used to deposit shoes since worshippers and visitors must remove them.

Label: Enter the inner mosque
Description: A single prayer mat faces the qibla, the niche in the wall indicating the direction to Makkah (Mecca). The mat would be used by the imam (prayer leader). An imam who leads prayers for the juma namaz (Friday congregational prayer) might use the steps on the right to present the kutba (“sermon”).

Label: Check the calendar for prayer times
Description: An Islamic prayer calendar indicates the prayer times each day as they shift with the timing of sunrise, high noon, and sunset.

Label: N to DD
Description: This trail leaves the small neighborhood in which the Sayyid family lives and heads north into other muhallas.

Label: N to M
Description: The concrete-covered brick buildings and well paved gali (“alley”) evidence the relative wealth in this part of Chainpur.

Label: View a Quran
Description: Sayyid Umar holds a Quran portion. During the month of Ramzan (Ramadan) when Muslims celebrate the revelation of the Quran, many Muslims will read 1/30th of this Arabic-language text per day, completing it by Id (the day marking the end of the month). This edition of the Quran divides it into thirty parts to facilitate this.
